study.title: Joshua 14 The Dealled Heritage and the Persevering Faith of Caleb
study.overview: Joshua 14 shows two realities connected with each other: the orderly distribution of the promised land between the tribes and the special concession of Caleb's inheritance in Hebron. The chapter emphasizes that the division did not occur by human improvisation, but according to the command of the LORD, with priestly, civil and tribal leadership. In the midst of this scenario, Caleb emerges as an example of persevering faith: even old, he claims the promise received decades earlier, trusts that God is still with him and receives Hebron. The closure of the chapter highlights the rest of the earth after the wars, pointing to the partial fulfillment of the divine promise at that time.

outline.title: The division of the earth under the direction of God
outline.explanation: The inheritance in the land of Canaan is distributed by Eleazar, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes, according to the commandment given by God through Moses. The text highlights that the process was done by luck, showing dependence on divine decision and not human preferences. He also explains why the Levites did not receive tribal territory: their inheritance would be different, with cities for housing and sustenance.

outline.title: Caleb claims promise with faith and vigor
outline.explanation: Caleb reminds Joshua of what the LORD promised because of his faithfulness when he was sent to recognize the land. He contrasts his posture with that of the spies that discouraged the people and states that he continued following the Lord. Even eighty-five years old, he declares that his strength is still sufficient for the mission, asks for the Mount of Hebron and recognizes that victory depends on God's presence.

outline.title: Hebron is granted and the earth rests
outline.explanation: Joshua blesses Caleb and grants him Hebron as an inheritance. The text reinforces that this possession was the result of his fidelity to the Lord. In mentioning the ancient name Quiriate-Arba and the rest of wars, the chapter links local history to the advancement of God's plan for Israel.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the period of the occupation of the land of Canaan through Israel. The text reports that the distribution took place in Gilgal, which at that time served as the center of command of the people. The mention of Eleazar, the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes indicates a community and religious organization to divide the land with justice and according to the divine order. Also appears the contrast between the tribes that received inheritance west of the Jordan and those who had already received territory on the other side of the river, in addition to the unique situation of the Levites, who did not receive a tribal territory of their own.
study.theology: Joshua 14 teaches that God's promise does not lapse in time or with human age. The inheritance is distributed according to the word of the LORD, and luck functions as an instrument of submission to the divine government. The absence of territory for the Levites shows that God's provision can take different forms for different groups within the people. In Caleb, the text highlights persevering faith, memory of promises and practical trust: he not only believes, but asks, acts and faces obstacles. Hebron's concession shows that fidelity to God is taken into account in the way the promise is enjoyed, without turning it into autonomous merit, for Caleb himself attributes victory to the presence of the LORD. The final rest of the earth anticipates the restoration and peace that God gives to his people.

scholarViews.insight: The whole section is framed by the distribution of the earth, with Caleb at the beginning and Joshua at the end, highlighting the only two men who remained faithful at the time of the spy.
Caleb presents his claim of Hebron before the general draw, as a reward promised for his faithfulness when he brought a report of faith in Cades-Barnea.
Hebron is granted to Caleb, and the ancient name Quiriate-Arba is linked to the meaning of "the city of four," possibly related to notable figures among the Anakim.

questions: What does the distribution of the earth by luck teach about the way God conducts apparently administrative decisions?
In what respects Caleb's perseverance confronts the tendency to give up when the promise takes time to be fulfilled?
How does Hebron's concession show that faith, memory and practical action need to walk together?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to trust that God remains faithful when time passes and circumstances seem difficult. The practical application is to remember biblical promises, persevere in service even in old age or in delay, and act courageously in the face of obstacles that seem too great. It also calls on the community to treat common decisions with justice, order and submission to God's will, rather than favoritism or anxiety.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text does not explain in detail the exact method of the draw or describes the complete geography of Hebron here. Adam Clarke's observation of Quiriate-Arba's sense as "city of the four" is interpretative and presented as a hypothesis, not as a certainty of the text. Nor should we say, based on this chapter, all the historical details of Gilgal or the exact composition of the tribal council beyond what the text itself informs.
